The most powerful refutation is the “swine objection” (Mill’s reply to Bentham): if pleasures differ only in quantity, a satisfied pig’s life could rank above a dissatisfied Socrates’s, which clashes with our considered judgments about higher and lower pleasures. This exposes the calculus’s failure to capture qualitative distinctions and its implausible reduction of all value to a single hedonic scale. The claim that pain and pleasure are inevitable features of life does not refute the calculus, since Bentham’s method concerns comparing and summing pleasures and pains, not eliminating them.
CONFIDENCE: 88
